purpose: Repaint the older Sikh films reused in wave 1 (month one) so no two look the same (owner: "We can't have the same look for every film... You don't go to AMC and watch a movie that looks like the last one").
rules: no two Sikh month-one films within 3 days of each other share a look (new or reused); neighbouring days never match
each shot keeps its story beat and framing from the existing art; only the look changes (the old still is uploaded to ChatGPT as the layout reference)
no text in images unless the look needs it; vertical 9:16; no rainbow gradients
today shots get a diverse modern cast
no faces of the Sikh Gurus: from behind, hands, silhouette or light only
neighbours: new month-one Sikh films: 9 chrome, 21 film35, 28 inkwash, 29 phulkari, 30 miniature.

shots.name: SW1-Puri-Shore
shots.beat: Long ago, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana, a Muslim musician, walked to Puri, a temple town by the sea in eastern India.

shots.name: SW2-Temple-Lamps
shots.beat: At dusk the priests lifted golden trays of lamps, flowers and incense, and waved them in worship. It’s called aarti.

shots.name: SW3-Standing-Apart
shots.beat: Guru Nanak didn’t join in. The puzzled priests came out and asked him why.

shots.name: SW4-Sky-Tray
shots.beat: He pointed up and sang. The sky is the tray. The sun and moon are the lamps. The stars are the pearls.

shots.name: SW5-Song-Under-Stars
shots.beat: Mardana played, and Guru Nanak kept singing: sandalwood on the wind is the incense, the forests are the flowers. The whole world is already doing aarti.

shots.name: SW6-Today-Window
shots.beat: Sikhs still sing that song every night. And when something is bigger than words, they say Waheguru: wow, the teacher.
shots.cast: a Sikh woman in a turban in Surrey, Canada

shots.name: ZSB1-Goindwal-Langar
shots.beat: In the village of Goindwal, the third Guru, Guru Amar Das, kept a kitchen where everyone ate together, sitting in rows on the floor.

shots.name: ZSB2-Emperor-Arrives
shots.beat: One day a visitor arrived with a crowd of courtiers: Akbar, the Mughal emperor, the most powerful man in India.

shots.name: ZSB3-Emperor-Sits
shots.beat: The custom was: first sit in the row, then meet the Guru. So the emperor sat on the floor between farmers and the poor, and ate the same plain meal.

shots.name: ZSB4-The-Offer
shots.beat: Afterward, Akbar offered the Guru land, so the kitchen would never run short. In most tellings, the Guru gently said no.

shots.name: ZSB5-Sangat-Gives
shots.beat: The kitchen, he said, belongs to the sangat. It runs on what ordinary people give, and on the hands that cook and serve.

shots.name: ZSB6-Today-Door
shots.beat: Today every gurdwara, “the door of the Guru,” is open to anyone. Cover your head, take off your shoes, wash your hands, and come in.
shots.cast: a Sikh grandfather welcoming neighbours of every background in Melbourne

shots.name: SC1-Patna-River
shots.beat: Long ago in Patna, by the river Ganges, a little boy played on the riverbank. He would grow up to be the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh.
shots.problem: WRONG PICTURE in clips/: a mislabelled image from another shot was rendered here. Restore this shot from pre-repaint/.

shots.name: SC2-Bangle-Splash
shots.beat: One day he slipped off his gold bangle and tossed it into the river.

shots.name: SC3-Mother-Asks
shots.beat: His mother hurried down to the water. Where did it fall? Show me.

shots.name: SC4-Second-Bangle
shots.beat: So he tossed in the other one too. Right there, he said.

shots.name: SC5-Crowns-For-All
shots.beat: In his day, fine turbans marked kings and nobles. The Guru asked every Sikh to keep their hair and cover it. A crown for every family.

shots.name: SC6-Today-Mirror
shots.beat: Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut, called kesh, and tie a turban, the dastaar, fresh each morning. On the wrist, a kara: plain steel.
shots.cast: a young Sikh man in Nairobi

shots.name: SP1-Anandpur-Crowd
shots.beat: Vaisakhi, 1699. A huge crowd gathered at Anandpur for the spring harvest festival. Guru Gobind Singh raised a sword and asked: who will give their head for the faith?

shots.name: SP2-One-Man-Stands
shots.beat: Silence. Then one man stood: Daya Ram, a shopkeeper from Lahore.

shots.name: SP3-The-Tent
shots.beat: The Guru led him into a tent and came out alone. He asked again. What happened inside? The tellings differ.

shots.name: SP4-Four-More
shots.beat: Four more stood, one at a time: a farmer, a water-carrier, a cloth printer and a barber, from far corners of India.

shots.name: SP5-Five-Return
shots.beat: Then all five walked out alive, dressed alike, beside the Guru. Sikhs call them the Panj Pyare: the five beloved.

shots.name: SP6-Steel-Bowl
shots.beat: They drank amrit, water and sugar stirred with a double-edged sword in one steel bowl. Then the Guru asked the five to give him amrit too.

shots.name: SA1-Dusty-Field
shots.beat: In Guru Gobind Singh’s time, during the battles at Anandpur, wounded and thirsty soldiers lay in the dust on both sides.

shots.name: SA2-Water-Bag
shots.beat: An old Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya walked among them with a leather water bag, giving each one a drink.

shots.name: SA3-Both-Sides
shots.beat: He gave water to everyone. Sikh soldiers, and the enemy’s soldiers too.

shots.name: SA4-Before-The-Guru
shots.beat: Some Sikhs were angry. They brought him to Guru Gobind Singh. He’s helping the enemy!

shots.name: SA5-The-Balm
shots.beat: The Guru was pleased. He gave Ghanaiya a soothing balm. Keep giving water, he said, and ease their wounds too.

shots.name: SA6-Ardas-Today
shots.beat: Today, Sikhs end their standing prayer, the Ardas, with three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all.
shots.cast: a Sikh family of every age in Birmingham, UK

shots.name: SV1-Dawn-River
shots.beat: Guru Nanak, a young man working in the town of Sultanpur, went to bathe in the river Bein one morning, as he always did.

shots.name: SV2-Searching-Banks
shots.beat: He didn’t come out. The town searched the banks for three days.

shots.name: SV3-Out-Of-The-Water
shots.beat: On the third day he walked out of the water and said: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.

shots.name: SV4-Town-Square
shots.beat: The town’s governor and its judge, the qazi, heard about it. Then come and pray with us, they said.

shots.name: SV5-At-Prayer
shots.beat: At prayer time Nanak stood with them in the mosque, but didn’t bow. Afterwards they asked him why.

shots.name: SV6-Today-Street
shots.beat: Sikh means a learner. Guru Nanak’s path grew into a faith of its own. Not Hindu, not Muslim, and it puts neither down.
shots.cast: a Sikh woman in a turban with friends on a Delhi street

shots.name: SK1-Two-Swords
shots.beat: When Guru Hargobind became the sixth Guru, still very young, he asked for not one sword but two.

shots.name: SK2-Riders-In-The-Hills
shots.beat: Years later, riding with his Sikhs through the hills, he met a famous wandering holy man, Samarth Ramdas.

shots.name: SK3-Holy-Man-Asks
shots.beat: The holy man asked: you sit on Guru Nanak’s seat. Why ride with swords and horses?

shots.name: SK4-The-Answer
shots.beat: Inside, a hermit, the Guru said. Outside, a prince. The sword is to protect the poor and stand up to cruelty.

shots.name: SK5-Flag
shots.beat: Today two curved swords wrap around the Khanda, the symbol on the Sikh flag: a circle, and a double-edged sword in the middle.

shots.name: SK6-Today-Desk
shots.beat: The circle has no beginning and no end, like the one God. The middle sword cuts truth from lies. The two outside: world and spirit, held together.
shots.cast: a Sikh woman engineer in Seattle

shots.name: SE1-River-At-Dawn
shots.beat: Long ago, an old man named Amar Das walked to the river every morning before dawn, to fill a pitcher of water for his teacher, Guru Angad.

shots.name: SE2-Long-Walk-Back
shots.beat: He carried it a long way back to the village of Khadur, so the Guru could bathe. He did it for years, and never asked for thanks.

shots.name: SE3-Stormy-Night
shots.beat: One stormy night, in the dark and the rain, he tripped beside a weaver’s hut and fell. He kept hold of the pitcher.

shots.name: SE4-Weavers-Wife
shots.beat: Inside, the weaver’s wife grumbled: that must be Amru nithaavan, homeless old Amru, with no place of his own.

shots.name: SE5-Home-Of-The-Homeless
shots.beat: Guru Angad said: he is not homeless. He is the home of the homeless. In time, he chose Amar Das as the third Guru.

shots.name: SE6-Today-Langar
shots.beat: Today, in gurdwaras everywhere, people still serve like this: shoes handed back, plates scrubbed, roti rolled by someone you’ll never meet.
shots.cast: Sikh volunteers and helpers of many backgrounds in a New York langar kitchen

shots.name: SB1-Roadside-Inn
shots.beat: On one of his journeys, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana stopped at a roadside inn run by a man named Sajjan.

shots.name: SB2-The-Host
shots.beat: Sajjan seemed so holy. He had built a temple for his Hindu guests and a mosque for his Muslim guests, and welcomed every traveler.

shots.name: SB3-Night-Song
shots.beat: That night, Guru Nanak asked Mardana to play, and he sang. Sajjan, waiting in the dark, stopped to listen.

shots.name: SB4-Bronze-Bowl
shots.beat: The song said: bronze is bright and shiny, but rub it, and its blackness shows. Wash it a hundred times, and it still won’t come clean.

shots.name: SB5-Sajjan-Kneels
shots.beat: Sajjan knew the song was about him. He fell at the Guru’s feet, told the truth, and gave what he had stolen to the poor.

shots.name: SB6-Today-True-Words
shots.beat: At the top of the Sikh scripture, God is called Sat Naam: truth is the name. Sat means what really is, not what shines.
shots.cast: a Sikh man in a turban and his Black colleague in Toronto

shots.name: SR1-Hot-Hills
shots.beat: On a blazing day in the hills, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana were walking. Mardana was desperately thirsty, and there was no water anywhere.

shots.name: SR2-Spring-On-Top
shots.beat: At the top of the hill, beside the only spring, sat a Sufi holy man, Wali Qandhari. Mardana climbed up and asked for a drink.

shots.name: SR3-New-Spring
shots.beat: The Guru told Mardana to lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and fresh water bubbled up. Up at the top, the old spring began to dry.

shots.name: SR4-Boulder
shots.beat: The holy man was furious. He pushed a huge boulder down the hill, straight at them.

shots.name: SR5-Handprint
shots.beat: Guru Nanak raised his open hand and stopped it. Many Sikhs say his handprint is still in the rock today.

shots.name: SR6-Today-Calm
shots.beat: The Sikh root verse says God is nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Sikhs take it as a picture of who a person can become.
shots.cast: a Sikh dad in a patka with his daughter in Southall

shots.name: LA1-Carpenters-Yard
shots.beat: In the town of Saidpur, Guru Nanak stayed with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who earned every coin with his own two hands.

shots.name: LA2-Plain-Bread
shots.beat: Lalo shared what he had: coarse, plain bread. The Guru ate it gladly.

shots.name: LA3-Rich-Feast
shots.beat: Across town, a rich official, Malik Bhago, threw a great feast for holy men. Everyone came, except Guru Nanak.

shots.name: LA4-Summoned
shots.beat: Bhago was insulted, and sent for him. Why do you eat a poor man’s bread and refuse mine?

shots.name: LA5-Two-Breads
shots.beat: He took Lalo’s bread in one hand and Bhago’s rich food in the other, and squeezed.

shots.name: LA6-Today-Workshop
shots.beat: Sikhs call this kirat karni: honest work. Earn your living by your own effort, without cheating anyone.
shots.cast: a Sikh mechanic in Fresno and a Latina customer

shots.name: DN1-Lahore-Mansion
shots.beat: In Lahore lived a very rich man named Duni Chand. Over his house flew flags, one for every hundred thousand rupees he owned.

shots.name: DN2-The-Visit
shots.beat: When Guru Nanak came to visit, Duni Chand showed him everything, and asked: is there anything I can do for you?

shots.name: DN3-The-Needle
shots.beat: The Guru handed him a small sewing needle. Keep this for me, he said. Give it back to me in the next world.

shots.name: DN4-Wife-Asks
shots.beat: His wife asked: how will you take a needle with you when you die? Nobody can take anything.

shots.name: DN5-Sharing
shots.beat: So Duni Chand began to share: food and money for the hungry, given with his own hands.

shots.name: DN6-Today-Portion
shots.beat: Sikhs call this vand chakna: share, then eat. Many set aside a tenth of what they earn for others, called dasvandh.

shots.name: ZSO1-Dark-Forest
shots.beat: On their travels, Mardana once wandered off alone into a deep forest, looking for food.

shots.name: ZSO2-Kauda
shots.beat: There lived Kauda, a fierce man every traveler feared. He caught Mardana, tied him up, and set a huge pot of oil over the fire to throw him in.

shots.name: ZSO3-The-Song
shots.beat: Guru Nanak came into the clearing and began to sing. Tradition says that however high the fire burned, the oil would not boil. It stayed cool.

shots.name: ZSO4-Kauda-Kneels
shots.beat: Kauda fell at the Guru’s feet and wept. He let Mardana go, and changed his ways. The fiercest man in the forest came out a new one.

shots.name: ZSO5-Bein-Dawn
shots.beat: Remember the river Bein? Sikhs say Guru Nanak came out of it with a charge: remember the Name, and help others remember. In the forest, that’s what he did.

shots.name: ZSO6-Today-Water
shots.beat: many sikhs bathe before their dawn prayers, the way guru nanak went to the river each morning. today, when you let water run, at a tap or in the shower, bring to mind a time you went into something hard and came out different. you don’t have to understand it. just say thank you, in whatever way is yours.
shots.cast: a young Malaysian Sikh man in Kuala Lumpur

shots.name: ZSA1-Rude-Village
shots.beat: On his travels, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana came to a village where nobody would welcome them. People mocked them and shut their doors.

shots.name: ZSA2-Stay-Settled
shots.beat: As they left, the Guru turned and blessed the village: may you stay settled here, always.

shots.name: ZSA3-Warm-Village
shots.beat: At the next village, people ran out to meet them. They fed them, sang hymns with them, and gave them a place to sleep.

shots.name: ZSA4-Scatter
shots.beat: As they left, he blessed them: may you be scattered. Mardana stopped in the road. Master, why bless the cruel to stay and the kind to scatter?

shots.name: ZSA5-Seeds-On-Wind
shots.beat: The Guru said: let the unkind stay where they are, so their ways don’t spread. Let the good scatter, and carry goodness wherever they go.

shots.name: ZSA6-Today-Sangat
shots.beat: Sikhs call it sangat: the company you keep. The stories say that wherever Guru Nanak went, he left a small circle behind, to sing and share food.

shots.name: SD1-Pool-Amritsar
shots.beat: Over four hundred years ago, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, began building a house of God in the middle of a sacred pool in Amritsar.

shots.name: SD2-First-Stone
shots.beat: Many Sikhs tell that he asked his friend, the Muslim saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to lay the first stone.

shots.name: SD3-Four-Doors
shots.beat: And he gave it four doors, one on every side. You could walk in from any direction.

shots.name: SD4-The-Book
shots.beat: Then Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus into one great book, with songs by Hindu and Muslim saints in it too.

shots.name: SD5-Ik-Onkar
shots.beat: The book opens with Guru Nanak’s symbol, Ik Onkar. Ik is written as the numeral one. Onkar is an ancient name for God.

shots.name: SD6-Today-Golden-Temple
shots.beat: Today, at the Golden Temple, the doors still face every way, and the great book is still carried in each morning.

shots.name: ZSC1-Night-Escape
shots.beat: Winter, 1704. After years of war, Guru Gobind Singh had lost his home at Anandpur. His companions were scattered, and two of his sons had died in battle.

shots.name: ZSC2-Earth-Pillow
shots.beat: He walked alone into the forest of Machhiwara, his feet torn and bare. Tradition says he lay on the cold ground, with a lump of earth for a pillow.

shots.name: ZSC3-Song-At-Dawn
shots.beat: And there, tradition says, he sang a hymn Sikhs still sing today: go and tell the beloved Friend how his people are.

shots.name: ZSC4-Friends-Find
shots.beat: At dawn his Sikhs found him, and two Muslim brothers, Ghani Khan and Nabi Khan, helped carry him to safety.

shots.name: ZSC5-Chardi-Kala
shots.beat: Sikhs call it chardi kala: ever-rising spirits. Not pretending it’s fine. Choosing which way your spirit faces, even when things fall.

shots.name: ZSC6-Today-Grandfather
shots.beat: today, when someone asks how you are, try telling the truth, and then one thing that still lifts you. many sikhs answer with just two words: chardi kala.

films.suffix: loose watercolour and ink wash, bleeding pigment, confident black ink linework, generous white paper, bold saturated pigment blooms, strong black ink, vivid not pale
films.why: a Sufi friend's loss and loyalty: bold ink and watercolour
films.todayCast: a Sikh woman lawyer in London

shots.name: ZSD1-Pir-Arrives
shots.beat: In the hills lived a Muslim Sufi saint, Pir Budhu Shah, a close friend of Guru Gobind Singh. When the Guru’s people were attacked, he came to stand with them.

shots.name: ZSD2-Combing
shots.beat: Afterward, the Pir found the Guru combing his long, uncut hair with a small wooden comb, as Sikhs do each morning.

shots.name: ZSD3-The-Request
shots.beat: Ask for anything, the Guru said. The Pir pointed to the comb, with a few hairs still caught in it. That one, please.

shots.name: ZSD4-The-Gift
shots.beat: The Guru gave him the comb with the hair, and with it, tradition says, a small sword and a turban. His family kept them as treasures for generations.

shots.name: ZSD5-Five-Ks
shots.beat: Initiated Sikhs carry five such things, the five Ks: kesh, uncut hair. Kanga, a comb. Kara, a steel bracelet. Kachera, cotton undershorts. Kirpan, a small sword.

shots.name: ZSD6-Today-Kara
shots.beat: today, choose one thing you already wear, a ring, a watch, a hair tie, and give it a job: when you touch it, remember who you mean to be. sikhs do this with the kara.
shots.cast: a Sikh woman lawyer in London

shots.name: ZSE1-Pandits-Arrive
shots.beat: 1675. A group of Hindu pandits from Kashmir arrived at Anandpur, worn out. Back home, they were being forced to give up their faith.

shots.name: ZSE2-Guru-Listens
shots.beat: They begged the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, for help. He listened, and grew quiet. Tradition says he told them it would take the sacrifice of a great soul.

shots.name: ZSE3-Boy-Asks
shots.beat: His son Gobind, nine years old, asked what was wrong. Then he said: who is greater than you, father, to do this?

shots.name: ZSE4-Road-To-Delhi
shots.beat: So the Guru went to Delhi to speak for their freedom. He would not give up his faith, or let theirs be taken. There he was put to death.

shots.name: ZSE5-Sis-Ganj
shots.beat: Sikhs honor him as a martyr for other people’s freedom. A gurdwara, Sis Ganj, stands in Delhi where he died.

shots.name: ZSE6-Today-Stand-Up
shots.beat: today, notice one person near you who believes differently, and quietly be on their side: include them, speak up for them, or ask about their faith with real interest.

shots.name: ZSF1-Godavari
shots.beat: 1708. By the river Godavari at Nanded, far in the south, Guru Gobind Singh knew his life was ending. His Sikhs gathered, wondering who would lead them next.

shots.name: ZSF2-Granth
shots.beat: He had the scripture brought out: the hymns of the Gurus, first gathered by Guru Arjan a century before.

shots.name: ZSF3-Coins-Coconut
shots.beat: Before it he placed five coins and a coconut, the old sign of handing on the Guruship. Then he bowed.

shots.name: ZSF4-Guru-Bows
shots.beat: From now on, he told them, there would be no more human Gurus. Your Guru is the Granth, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib.

shots.name: ZSF5-Put-To-Rest
shots.beat: So it’s treated like a revered teacher: above everyone, under a canopy. At night it’s wrapped and carried to rest. At dawn it’s opened again.

shots.name: ZSF6-Today-Dawn
shots.beat: today, if you like, read the hukamnama, the order of the day, that the golden temple shares online each morning. many sikhs read it like a letter from the guru. read it, or just listen. your choice.

shots.name: ZSH1-Talwandi
shots.beat: Spring, 1469, in Punjab. A mud-brick village called Talwandi sat among the wheat fields, southwest of Lahore.

shots.name: ZSH2-Landlord-Accountant
shots.beat: Its landlord was a Muslim, Rai Bular. His village accountant was a Hindu, Mehta Kalu. And Kalu’s wife, Mata Tripta, was about to have a baby.

shots.name: ZSH3-Birth-Light
shots.beat: The old stories say that when the baby came, the little room filled with light. The midwife, a Muslim woman named Daultan, said she’d never seen a child like him.

shots.name: ZSH4-Big-Sister
shots.beat: His big sister, Nanaki, was about five. The baby was named Nanak.

shots.name: ZSH5-Nankana-Today
shots.beat: Talwandi is now called Nankana Sahib, Nanak’s town, in Pakistan. A gurdwara stands where tradition says he was born, and Sikh pilgrims still travel there.

shots.name: ZSH6-Today-Beginning
shots.beat: today, ask someone who was there about one small detail of your beginning: the weather, the room, who came first. every story starts somewhere small. yours too.

shots.name: ZSJ1-Dreamy-Boy
shots.beat: In Talwandi, young Nanak worried the grown-ups. He gave things away, sat silent for hours, and asked questions nobody could answer.

shots.name: ZSJ2-Sister-Watches
shots.beat: His father loved him and worried constantly. But his big sister, Nanaki, watched him differently. She believed in him before there was much to go on.

shots.name: ZSJ3-Sultanpur-Home
shots.beat: Nanaki married and moved to the town of Sultanpur. When her brother was a young man, drifting, she brought him there, and her husband found him work.

shots.name: ZSJ4-The-Rabab
shots.beat: Some tellings say that when he set out, Nanaki gave the money for Mardana’s rabab, the instrument that would carry her brother’s songs.

shots.name: ZSJ5-Promise
shots.beat: Before he left, tradition says, he promised her: whenever you remember me, I’ll come. Years later, at the end of her life, he came.

shots.name: ZSJ6-Today-Note
shots.beat: today, send one line to someone who saw you first, before there was much to go on. just: i remember what you did. thank you.
shots.cast: a young Sikh man in Melbourne

films.suffix: layered paper cut-out collage, cut and torn coloured paper, visible paper fibres and soft drop shadows, handmade diorama depth, bright saturated paper colours, lime, pink, saffron and cobalt
films.why: a village school: paper cut-out
films.todayCast: a Sikh dad and his daughter in Auckland

shots.name: ZSK1-To-School
shots.beat: When Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher, the pandha, to learn his letters and one day keep accounts like his dad.

shots.name: ZSK2-Wooden-Board
shots.beat: The teacher wrote the alphabet on a wooden board, a patti, and told the boy to copy it. Nanak did.

shots.name: ZSK3-The-Question
shots.beat: Then he asked: but what do they mean? Not what sound they make. What do they point to? The teacher had no answer.

shots.name: ZSK4-Boy-Explains
shots.beat: So the boy began to explain. Each letter could point toward God. The first, toward the One who made everything. The next, toward truth. And on and on.

shots.name: ZSK5-Teacher-Bows
shots.beat: In the story, the teacher bowed to his student.

shots.name: ZSK6-Today-Question
shots.beat: today, take one word you use every day, home, sorry, friend, and ask nanak’s question of it: what does this really point to? let it open slowly.
shots.cast: a Sikh dad and his daughter in Auckland

films.why: a cobra shading a sleeping boy: Kalighat snakes
films.todayCast: a Sikh woman in her sixties in Punjab

shots.name: ZSL1-Buffaloes
shots.beat: A hot afternoon beyond Talwandi. Young Nanak had been sent to watch the family’s buffaloes. His father hoped it would teach him responsibility.

shots.name: ZSL2-Asleep
shots.beat: But the boy lay down under a tree and fell asleep in the heat. Slowly the sun moved, and the shade slid off his face.

shots.name: ZSL3-Cobra-Hood
shots.beat: A cobra slid up beside him, raised itself, and spread its hood wide over his face, like a small umbrella.

shots.name: ZSL4-Rai-Bular-Sees
shots.beat: Rai Bular, the village landlord, came riding by and saw it. He didn’t reach for a stick. He understood that this boy was under God’s protection.

shots.name: ZSL5-Rai-Bular-Honors
shots.beat: From that day, Rai Bular honored the boy, and defended him to his worried father more than once.

shots.name: ZSL6-Today-Shade
shots.beat: today, if you can, sit in some shade for two minutes: a tree, a porch, the cool side of a room. bring to mind one time you were sheltered without arranging it, and say thank you, to god or to life. your choice.
shots.cast: a Sikh woman in her sixties in Punjab

films.suffix: South Asian truck-art painting, glossy enamel colours, hot pink, emerald, gold and electric blue, ornate floral borders, peacocks and mirror-inlay sparkle, bold folk outlines, celebratory and loud
films.why: twenty rupees at the market: Punjabi truck art

shots.name: SL1-Father-Coins
shots.beat: When Guru Nanak was young, his father gave him twenty rupees and sent him to market. Make a good deal, he said. A true bargain.

shots.name: SL2-Hungry-Holy-Men
shots.beat: On the road, Nanak met a group of holy men who had gone without food for days.

shots.name: SL3-Shared-Meal
shots.beat: He spent every rupee on flour, lentils and ghee, and fed them all.

shots.name: SL4-Empty-Hands
shots.beat: He came home with empty hands. His father was furious. Where’s the deal?

shots.name: SL5-Emperor-In-The-Row
shots.beat: Sikh tradition says that when the emperor Akbar came to see the third Guru, he first sat on the floor and ate in the row with everyone.

shots.name: SL6-Today-Langar
shots.beat: Today gurdwaras everywhere keep a langar, a free kitchen. Simple vegetarian food, everyone in one row on the floor, the pangat. Any faith, or none.

films.suffix: 1990s music-video VHS still, chromatic aberration, scan lines, tape noise, saturated colour, handheld low-angle energy, hot magenta and cyan colour bleed, high energy
films.why: tera, tera at the grain scale: music-video VHS

shots.name: TR1-Grain-Store
shots.beat: As a young man in Sultanpur, Guru Nanak worked as a storekeeper, weighing out grain from the governor’s store.

shots.name: TR2-Counting
shots.beat: One day he was measuring grain for a customer, counting each measure aloud: one, two, three…

shots.name: TR3-Tera
shots.beat: At thirteen he said tera, and stopped counting. Tera, tera, he kept saying, yours, yours, and kept pouring out the grain.

shots.name: TR4-Complaint
shots.beat: Someone ran to the governor: Nanak is giving away the store! The governor ordered the accounts checked.

shots.name: TR5-Accounts
shots.beat: The clerks counted everything. Nothing was missing. In many tellings, there was even more than before.

shots.name: TR6-Today-Breath
shots.beat: Sikhs build a life on three pillars: naam japna, remembering God all day long. Kirat karni, honest work. And vand chakna, sharing.
